unverified: The sequence of the example case (wholesaler portal, Sunday 11:14 p.m., password cracked elsewhere, decision years ago) is invented and marked as an example.

Newly checked 02.11.2026: S1 (access to an email account lets criminals take over other services by resetting passwords; second factor for important accounts such as email), S2 (two-step verification on the password manager too; strong, separate password for email) and S3 (new password, end all active sessions, check other accounts; the checklist covers handed-over login details and is applied here to a taken-over account).
The NCSC names two-step verification as the most important first step; this video centres on the password manager and mentions the second factor only to protect the manager.

beats.spoken: Monday, 7:50 a.m. An email from your wholesaler: your password has been changed. It wasn't you. And you use the same password for your email account.

Let's rewind. Sunday night, someone logs in with your password. Weeks ago, it was cracked somewhere else. And years ago you decided: one strong password for every account. According to the BSI, criminals can then get into all of them.
What do you change? A: An even stronger password, again for everything. B: Just change the portal password. C: A password manager, one password per account. Remember your choice.

The right answer is C. The BSI says a separate, strong password for every account is safest. A password manager remembers them, protected by a master password and a second factor. Start with your email account. A and B leave the other accounts open.
Already taken over? Set a new password straight away and end all active sessions. Then check where the same password is still in use.
One password per account: those are the five minutes that were missing. What would you have picked? Tell me in the comments.
